sections.h2: Which Aitkin County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Two county offices share the work. The Assessor values and classifies every parcel, and the Treasurer bills and collects the money. The Assessor's Office answers at 218-927-7327. The Treasurer is at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431, and takes calls at 218-927-7325.

The Assessor's page says market value and classification are the main inputs to a tax bill, and that the office works under Minnesota statutes, Department of Revenue directives and County Board directives. A free parcel viewer called LINK shows basic parcel data. More detailed building records, including dimensions and sales reports, need a paid subscription, which the Assessor can explain by phone.

Anyone selling a house here will deal with both offices: the Assessor for value and class, the Treasurer for what is owed on the parcel before the deed changes hands.

sections.h2: What is it like to sell a house in Aitkin County?
sections.html:
Aitkin County is a lake-and-forest county in east central Minnesota, with Aitkin as the county seat. It covers 1,995 square miles, and 8.7% of that is water. The Mississippi River runs south through the middle of the county, the ground is wooded rolling hills, and Savanna Portage State Park and Rice Lake National Wildlife Refuge are among the protected areas on the map.

The county was set up in 1857 as Aiken County and took its present spelling in 1872. It was named for William Alexander Aitken, a fur trader for the American Fur Company, and it was organized in 1871. Winters are cold: the county seat averages a January low near 0 degrees Fahrenheit, and a record low of minus 47 was logged in January 1972.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table gives the market picture for the county:

  • 16,252 residents in July 2025, up 3.6% from the 2020 base, spread over about 8.6 people per square mile
  • 14,681 housing units, with 85.3% of homes owner-occupied
  • A median owner-occupied home value of $255,800 for 2020 to 2024
  • 35.7% of residents aged 65 or older, and a median household income of $60,833
  • 214 building permits issued in 2025, and a mean commute of 27.7 minutes

Those numbers describe a county where most people own their homes and more than a third of residents are 65 or older.

sections.h2: Is Aitkin County reassessing property for 2027?
sections.html:
Yes, in part of the county. The Assessor's page lists a 2027 reassessment in which appraisers began visiting in May 2026 and continue through the rest of the year. Inspections can fall anywhere between May 2026 and February 2027, so a visit may still be coming.

The areas on the list are Ball Bluff, Balsam, Fleming, Hazelton, Jevne, Macville, Malmo and Turner townships, unorganized territories 51-22, 52-24 and 52-25, and the city of Hill City. A reassessment means a physical inspection meant to verify and correct the county's records, and state law requires one for all taxable property at least once every five years.

An owner who wants to be present for the walk-through should call 218-927-7327 and mention any hazards on the property. A seller in one of these areas should expect the next valuation notice to reflect what the appraiser saw, which is another reason to keep records of recent repairs.

sections.h2: How do I appeal an Aitkin County valuation or classification?
sections.html:
Start by calling the Assessor, then move up the ladder only if that conversation does not settle it. The county's appeals page lays out the order:

  • Call or visit the Assessor's Office with your Notice of Valuation and Classification in hand.
  • Go to the Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, made up of the township board or city council, or to the Open Book meeting if your notice lists one. At Open Book, the assessors review the case and decide, and that decision can still go to the county board.
  • Appear before the County Board of Equalization in June. Book an appointment with the County Assessor first, and expect to have gone to the local board unless your area holds none.
  • Petition the Minnesota Tax Court. The county page gives April 30 of the year taxes are payable as the filing deadline, and says the Tax Court hears petitions even from owners who skipped the earlier steps.

Under Minnesota Statutes 274.01, local boards meet between April 1 and May 31, and they cannot trim the county's total assessment by more than one percent. Section 278.01 also lets an owner petition the district court by serving the county auditor, with filing due by April 30.

sections.h2: When are Aitkin County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Property tax is paid in two halves, due May 15 and October 15. The county's list of what to know before paying adds several details that apply to Aitkin County parcels:

Aitkin County tax payment points, from the county Treasurer's FAQ and Minnesota Statutes 279.01
ItemWhat applies
First halfDue before May 16
Second halfDue before October 16, with no second-half statement mailed
Mailed paymentCounts as on time if postmarked by the due date
Late penalty after the due date2% on homestead, 4% on nonhomestead
Delinquent statusAny tax unpaid before January 1 of the next year
Delinquent listPrinted in the newspaper each March

Because the county mails only one statement per parcel for the year, keep the stub for the second half. The Treasurer says a taxpayer stays responsible even when a statement never arrives, and the office sends courtesy letters with added penalty and fees when current-year taxes go unpaid. Statute 279.01 adds monthly penalties of one percent after the first jump, capped at 8% for homestead and 12% for nonhomestead property.

Statute 279.01 also treats a tax of $100 or less as one payment due with the first half. If your parcel is small, ask the Treasurer which threshold applies before you pay.

sections.h2: What happens to the Aitkin County tax bill when I sell?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's FAQ is blunt: any delinquent taxes must be paid at closing. Read your closing statement, or ask the realtor or attorney handling the sale, to see how the current year is split between buyer and seller.

If you escrow, your lender gets the tax figures from the county directly. The statement mailed to you is marked with bold text saying not to pay because taxes are escrowed, but it is still useful for tax filing and refund claims. A buyer who closes after the statement went out can get a copy online or from the Treasurer, and the county expects the new owner to make sure that copy reaches them.

Two state rules touch the deed itself. A certificate of value is required when real estate sells for more than $3,000 (Statute 272.115), and the assessor drops homestead classification after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies. The state deed tax on a sale above $3,000 is 0.33% of net consideration under Statute 287.21.

Manufactured homes follow their own track. Taxes must be paid before the title can transfer, and moving one requires a Mobile Home Clearance Sheet from the Treasurer showing current and delinquent taxes are paid.

sections.h2: Are there tax relief programs for Aitkin County homeowners?
sections.html:
Two programs come up on the county's pages. The first is the Minnesota Property Tax Refund, claimed on form M1PR from the Department of Revenue, which the Treasurer points owners to when they ask about eligibility.

The second is the Senior Citizen Property Tax Deferral. The county calls it a low-interest loan from the state and says it is not tax forgiveness. Homeowners aged 65 or older with household income of $60,000 or less can defer part of the tax, the state pays the county, and interest accrues. A seller already in the program should ask the Department of Revenue how a sale affects the deferred balance before listing.

Owners who are unsure whether a parcel qualifies for either program can call the Treasurer at 218-927-7325 and ask what documents to bring.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Aitkin County property tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Aitkin County Treasurer at 218-927-7325 for billing, payments and statement copies. The office is at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, in the city of Aitkin. Questions about value or classification go to the Assessor at 218-927-7327.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Aitkin County taxes by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer accepts a mailed payment as timely when the envelope is postmarked by the due date. Send it to 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431. Payment stubs also carry an address-change form on the back.

faqs.q: What if a tax statement never shows up?
faqs.a: You still owe the tax. The Treasurer states that the taxpayer remains responsible whether or not a statement arrives, and a copy can be pulled online or requested from the office. Late-payment penalties apply the same way.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay delinquent taxes before selling an Aitkin County house?
faqs.a: Yes. The county says delinquent taxes must be paid at closing. Any tax unpaid before January 1 of the following year is delinquent, so a seller with older balances should get a payoff figure from the Treasurer before the closing date.

faqs.q: Can I contest my Aitkin County valuation after the spring meetings?
faqs.a: Yes, through the Minnesota Tax Court. The Assessor's appeals page says the court hears petitions even from owners who skipped the local and county boards, with a filing deadline of April 30 of the year the taxes are payable.
